# Original ViT Against CNN Backbones: A Data, Architecture, and Task-Setting Review

## Abstract

This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with CNN backbones by architecture, data regime, task fit, and measured behavior. CNNs encode locality through shared sliding kernels and usually build hierarchical, multi-scale feature maps; plain ViT embeds non-overlapping patches and mixes tokens with global, content-dependent self-attention. The key empirical boundary is data scale: pure ViT can match or exceed CNNs such as ResNets and EfficientNet after ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M-scale pretraining, but may lag similarly sized CNNs on smaller data. Dense prediction is another boundary: original ViT is a patch-sequence classifier, whereas CNN backbones naturally expose pyramids. PVT, CvT, LeViT, HVT, and ViT-CoMer results therefore concern modified or hybrid designs, not unchanged ViT. Measured evidence supports conditional conclusions. CKA and attention-distance analyses show different representation propagation: ViTs have relatively uniform layer similarity and mixed local/global heads even early, while ResNets separate more strongly into stages and early CNN layers have fixed local receptive fields. Models with similar ImageNet accuracy can also differ in errors, calibration, transfer, invariance, and out-of-distribution behavior. Battle of the Backbones ties some supervised-CNN strength to larger datasets and describes ViTs as more sensitive to pretraining amount and parameter count. Thus the trade-off is between CNNs’ built-in locality and dense-prediction compatibility and ViT’s flexible global mixing, whose strongest results depend on scale, regularization, distillation, or downstream adaptation. ## Introduction

This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones, using architecture, training data, task fit, and measured behavior as the organizing choice rather than treating ImageNet accuracy as a universal ranking. The scope centers on plain ViT as introduced for image classification and on CNN feature extractors such as ResNet-style and later ConvNeXt-style backbones; hybrid, hierarchical, distilled, or otherwise modified transformers are relevant only when they expose a trade-off in the original comparison. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1]

The practical problem is backbone selection. A backbone is a pretrained or randomly initialized feature extractor used to build computer-vision systems, and for many years the default was an ImageNet-trained convolutional network. ViT changed this design space by applying a standard Transformer encoder to image patches, but its comparison with CNNs depends strongly on pretraining scale, model size, target task, and evaluation protocol. Battle of the Backbones makes this caution explicit: ImageNet classification alone does not determine which backbone is preferable across detection, out-of-distribution generalization, and other settings. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5]

The central architectural contrast is between convolution's built-in local processing and ViT's global content-dependent attention. CNNs share convolutional kernels over the image and build visual context through local receptive fields; ViT instead splits an image into fixed-length, non-overlapping patch tokens and applies multi-head self-attention followed by position-wise feed-forward layers. This gives ViT fewer vision-specific inductive biases than CNNs, which can aid flexibility at large scale but also creates a greater need for data or regularization. CvT's authors summarize the original empirical boundary in similar terms: pure Transformers can match or exceed ResNets and EfficientNet when trained on sufficiently large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, while ViT under similarly sized CNNs can lag when trained on smaller data. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1]

The comparison also cannot be reduced to classification-only performance. Plain ViT was designed primarily around a single patch sequence for classification, whereas CNN backbones commonly provide hierarchical, multi-scale feature maps useful for detection and segmentation. Later transformer work such as PVT introduced progressive shrinking and pyramid outputs specifically to make a convolution-free backbone usable for dense prediction; ViT-CoMer similarly attributes plain ViT's weak dense-prediction fit to limited inner-patch/local interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. These later systems are evidence of the original backbone's task boundary, not evidence that the original ViT itself already possessed those CNN-like pyramid properties. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:82373423792e] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:b632e07740d1]

Accordingly, the review will distinguish four questions: what each architecture encodes structurally, what data and training regime are needed for strong performance, how comparable results are under matched settings, and what limitations matter for deployment or downstream tasks. Reported wins will remain tied to their datasets, baselines, model sizes, pretraining, and metrics; results from hierarchical or hybrid transformers will not be used to rank plain ViT against CNNs where conditions are not directly comparable. ## Background and Method Taxonomy

Classification criteria for this review. This taxonomy organizes backbones by four linked comparison dimensions: feature locality and receptive-field growth, token or feature-map hierarchy, dependence on position encoding and pretraining, and suitability for classification versus dense prediction. These are review criteria for comparing the original ViT with CNN backbones, not a universal architecture taxonomy. They also do not equate model quality with inference efficiency: FLOPs, parameters, latency, hardware speed, memory, and edge-device deployment are related engineering dimensions, but each must be measured under its own setting. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:b33d5ca4d495] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214]

At the architectural pole, a standard CNN backbone is a local, weight-sharing feature extractor: convolutional kernels slide over the image, encode nearby spatial structure as an inductive bias, and typically expand receptive field through depth and downsampling. A plain ViT is a global, content-dependent sequence model: fixed non-overlapping image patches become tokens, and self-attention can relate distant token positions in every layer. CKA-based analysis supports treating these as functionally different representations rather than merely different parameterizations: ViTs show a comparatively uniform similarity structure across lower and higher layers, whereas ResNets separate representations more strongly into stages. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:0d7a530b916e] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:b1420373012c]

The locality criterion should not be read as “CNN local, ViT global at every head.” Measurements of ViT attention distance find a mixture of local and global heads even in the lowest self-attention layers, with higher layers becoming global; by contrast, early CNN layers have fixed local receptive fields. This distinction matters because it describes the mechanism by which context is aggregated, not the final accuracy. A later unified interpretation goes further and analyzes vision Transformers as input-conditioned, dynamic convolutions, but that analysis is a bridge between design spaces; it does not make the original ViT operationally identical to a fixed-kernel CNN backbone. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:5_local_and_global_information_in_layer_representations:0:41d4ea1578cc:claim:39e9842ac6c6] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:6b823b9a8c2a] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:a066cd8b17bb] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:644d231d8295]

The second axis is hierarchy. Classic CNN backbones naturally produce progressively lower-resolution, higher-semantic feature maps through convolutional strides and stage design, which is why they can be plugged into detection and segmentation frameworks. The original ViT instead maintains a patch-token sequence for classification and generally lacks the built-in multi-scale pyramid associated with ResNet-like backbones. PVT explicitly marks this difference: it introduces progressive shrinking and transformer feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32 so that a convolution-free transformer can replace CNN backbones for object detection and segmentation. Thus PVT, Swin-like systems, and other hierarchical transformers belong to a vision-specific transformer category, not to plain ViT. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:4d1864524c5a] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:a7f591fbce09]

The third axis is how spatial order and vision bias are supplied. The original ViT requires positional information because self-attention over a set is otherwise permutation invariant, while CNNs obtain spatial structure from local grid operations. Hybrid designs blur this boundary: CvT uses overlapping convolutional token embedding and convolutional projection in a multi-stage transformer and reports that positional encoding can be removed; LeViT borrows decreasing-resolution activation maps from CNNs and introduces attention bias for positional information. These are useful intermediate classes, but their results cannot be assigned to the original ViT or to pure CNNs without noting the hybrid mechanism. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:37:72d5be829727:claim:9fc9d95ec61d] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214]

The fourth axis is training and task regime. Plain ViT has fewer built-in visual biases and is more dependent on large-scale pretraining or strong regularization/distillation than CNNs; DeiT, for example, uses a CNN teacher together with stronger augmentation and regularization rather than relying only on the original large-dataset recipe. Task fit is also separate from architecture: classification evaluates a single predicted label, whereas detection and segmentation require localization and often multi-scale features. Battle of the Backbones reinforces this separation by benchmarking classification, detection, out-of-distribution behavior, calibration, transfer, and invariance rather than using ImageNet accuracy as a complete ranking. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5] [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:9b280ab2685b]

Under these criteria, the review uses three working groups. The first is plain ViT: a non-overlapping patch tokenizer, position encoding, a single-scale Transformer encoder, and global self-attention. The second is conventional CNN backbones: local convolution, shared kernels, staged downsampling, and hierarchical feature maps. The third is CNN–Transformer integration, including hierarchical vision transformers, convolutional tokenizers or projections, CNN-teacher distillation, and later multi-scale adapters. This grouping is intentionally comparative: it separates evidence about the original ViT–CNN contrast from evidence produced by designs created to combine their advantages. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:b632e07740d1]

Efficiency and deployment require a separate classification because the same architecture can look different by parameter count, FLOPs, measured latency, or hardware. HVT pools tokens to shorten the sequence and analogizes the reduction to CNN downsampling; LeViT explicitly evaluates speed/accuracy trade-offs across hardware and reports a CPU speed advantage over EfficientNet near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy; ED-ViT instead splits and prunes ViT models for multiple edge devices. These studies address compute or serving constraints, but they do not by themselves establish better representation quality, and latency results cannot be inferred from FLOPs or transferred across hardware. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:b33d5ca4d495]

Finally, task-specific hybrids should not be collapsed into the backbone comparison. PVT targets dense prediction by emulating a CNN feature pyramid without convolutions; ViT-CoMer keeps a plain pretrained ViT but injects convolutional multi-scale features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion for detection and segmentation; ConvLLaVA uses ConvNeXt as a visual encoder in a multimodal system to compress high-resolution image tokens. These are evidence that architecture choice interacts with output resolution, token redundancy, and downstream heads, but their numbers are comparable only within the stated task, dataset, pretraining, and model-size conditions. ## Representative Methods

Plain ViT mechanism. The original Vision Transformer treats image classification as sequence processing: an image is divided into fixed, non-overlapping patches, each patch is linearly embedded as a token, positional information is added, and repeated standard Transformer blocks use multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward networks to model relations among tokens. Its central contribution is not merely replacing convolution with attention, but showing that a pure Transformer encoder can be competitive with strong CNNs when visual training is conducted at sufficient scale. This applicability boundary is important: the architecture has comparatively few hand-designed vision biases, so its strongest case depends on large-scale pretraining or an alternative data-efficient training recipe rather than on convolution-like locality being built into every block. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] ViT's global aggregation differs from the staged processing of CNN backbones. In self-attention, each token can form input-dependent interactions with tokens across the image; empirical attention-distance analysis finds both local and global attention heads in the lowest ViT layers and global heads at higher layers. This gives plain ViT a direct route to long-range context, but it also means that locality, translation structure, and scale hierarchy are not imposed in the same explicit way as in a convolutional stack. The mechanism should therefore be interpreted as flexible, content-dependent mixing over a patch grid, not as a universal guarantee of better accuracy or efficiency. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:5_local_and_global_information_in_layer_representations:0:41d4ea1578cc:claim:39e9842ac6c6] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:6b823b9a8c2a] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:a066cd8b17bb] Representation evidence reinforces that ViT and ResNet-style CNNs process visual information differently. Centered kernel alignment comparisons show that ViTs have a relatively uniform internal representation structure, with greater similarity between lower and higher layers, whereas ResNet representations separate more clearly into lower and higher stages. In cross-model comparisons, many lower ResNet layers were needed to approximate representations found in a smaller portion of the lower ViT, while later portions of the two models mapped less directly. These findings support a functional distinction in representation propagation; they do not by themselves establish that one architecture produces universally superior features. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:0d7a530b916e] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:b1420373012c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6d5dc789edf3]

CNN backbone mechanism. Conventional CNN backbones use shared convolutional kernels that slide over a two-dimensional image, giving the model a strong locality and weight-sharing inductive bias. Stacked convolutional blocks expand the effective receptive field, while strides and stage transitions produce progressively lower-resolution feature maps with increasing channels. The CNN family is broad—including Inception-style multi-path blocks, ResNet, ResNeXt, DenseNet, EfficientNet, and later ConvNeXt-style designs—so comparisons should name the actual backbone rather than treating “CNN” as one fixed model. Their common contribution is a spatially local, hierarchical feature extractor that became the standard computer-vision backbone before transformer alternatives. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:10:88b24936d167:claim:c15fcfbfd547] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] The CNN mechanism is especially aligned with the structure of many vision tasks. Nearby pixels are usually correlated, and convolution directly encodes that local two-dimensional structure; repeated layers can combine local evidence into larger contexts. Stagewise downsampling also yields a feature pyramid at multiple strides, which detection and segmentation heads can use for small objects, fine boundaries, and semantically coarse regions. This is an architectural advantage for dense prediction, but it remains conditional on the task and implementation: a CNN backbone is not automatically more accurate than ViT, and a classification result does not prove equivalent performance under a detection or segmentation framework. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49]

Training-data contribution and boundary. The original ViT's evidence changed the meaning of architecture comparisons because data scale became a first-class variable. CvT's characterization of ViT is that pure Transformers can reach state-of-the-art image-classification performance relative to CNNs such as ResNets and EfficientNet on large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, but underperform similarly sized CNN counterparts when trained on smaller datasets. Thus, a ViT-versus-ResNet result obtained with JFT-scale pretraining is not directly comparable with a result from ImageNet-1K-only training, even if the model names and parameter counts look similar. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] DeiT identifies a different route to ViT applicability: data-efficient training and distillation rather than the original very-large-dataset regime. In the taxonomy used by LeViT's discussion, a convolutional teacher helps the transformer student acquire convolutional inductive bias, while stronger augmentation and regularization support training. This demonstrates that plain ViT's data dependence can be mitigated by training design, but it also separates the resulting evidence from the original ViT recipe: a distilled student should not be described as winning solely because of the unchanged architecture. The comparison with CNNs must therefore include the teacher, pretraining corpus, augmentations, and regularization. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44]

Battle of the Backbones provides a broader empirical framing of pretraining and architecture. Across its large suite of tasks, datasets, in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, and more than 1,500 training runs, supervised ConvNeXt, supervised SwinV2 trained with ImageNet-21k, and CLIP ViT-Base were highlighted as strong overall choices; the paper also reports that supervised CNNs trained on large sets performed best on most tasks among the models considered. Crucially, the authors attribute part of that supervised advantage to larger training datasets and report that self-supervised models are competitive in apples-to-apples comparisons at similar dataset scale. They also describe ViTs as more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. These are benchmark-specific findings about the included models and protocols, not a timeless ranking of all CNNs against all ViTs. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5]

Dense-prediction boundary of plain ViT. The original ViT was principally a classification architecture over a patch sequence, whereas practical CNN backbones had already been used as multi-scale feature extractors for pixel-level tasks. PVT states this contrast directly: unlike ViT's typically low-resolution outputs and high computational and memory cost, PVT is designed to train on dense image partitions, retain high output resolution, and use progressive shrinking to control the cost of large feature maps. Its transformer feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32 emulate the pyramid interface expected from ResNet-like CNN backbones. PVT is therefore evidence of what plain ViT lacked for dense prediction, not evidence that the original ViT already provided a CNN-style pyramid. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49] ViT-CoMer makes the same task-fit distinction from the opposite design direction: it retains a plain pretrained ViT but adds convolutional multi-receptive-field features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion. Its stated motivation is that plain ViT underperforms in dense prediction because it lacks inner-patch information interaction and has limited feature-scale diversity. The method injects a spatial pyramid of convolutional features and fuses hierarchical features across scales so that detection and segmentation can exploit both local and multi-scale information. Its applicability is therefore as an enhanced dense-prediction backbone that depends on added convolutional modules and available ViT pretraining; it should not be conflated with the original ViT baseline. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:82373423792e] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:b632e07740d1] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:a7f591fbce09]

Hierarchical and pooling transformers show how CNN design principles were reintroduced to address plain ViT limitations. HVT progressively pools visual tokens to reduce sequence length, drawing an explicit analogy to CNN feature-map downsampling; this permits scaling depth, width, resolution, or patch size while controlling compute, and its authors report that average-pooled tokens can be more discriminative than a single class token in their experiments. PVT instead builds a transformer pyramid without convolution. These methods preserve transformer-style token processing but modify the original single-sequence design, so their evidence concerns hierarchical transformers rather than plain ViT as originally specified. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49]

Convolution–Transformer hybrids form a separate method group. CvT introduces overlapping convolutional token embedding, a hierarchy of transformer stages, and convolutional projection inside transformer blocks, aiming to add CNN-like local context and shift, scale, and distortion robustness while retaining dynamic attention and global context. It also reports that these built-in convolutional structures allow positional encoding to be removed, simplifying adaptation to higher-resolution tasks. LeViT is another hybrid: it borrows decreasing-resolution activation maps from CNNs and uses attention bias to encode positional information, targeting fast inference rather than simply maximizing accuracy. Both methods combine mechanisms from the two families and therefore cannot be treated as either a pure CNN or the original ViT when interpreting results. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:37:72d5be829727:claim:9fc9d95ec61d] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:11:195dc7dad451:claim:1bb0a94cb919] The unified dynamic-convolution perspective offers an analytical bridge rather than an operational erasure of the architecture distinction. It interprets vision Transformers as ConvNets with input-conditioned dynamic convolutions, allowing attention and dynamic convolution design choices to be compared side by side and enabling designs such as replacing softmax with common ConvNet components or constructing a depth-wise vision Transformer. This helps explain relationships between content-dependent attention and convolution, but the original fixed-kernel CNN backbone still uses locally shared, index-defined kernels, while plain ViT's token mixing is global and content dependent. The appropriate conclusion is conceptual overlap and a shared design space, not identical inductive biases or identical deployment costs. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:6b823b9a8c2a] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:a066cd8b17bb] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:644d231d8295]

Efficiency mechanisms must be kept distinct from representational mechanisms. Plain global self-attention has cost that grows with the square of token count in the standard formulation, making higher-resolution inputs expensive; the dynamic-convolution survey explicitly identifies this quadratic complexity and slower vanilla-ViT convergence as reasons that CNN modules, pyramids, and local windows were brought back into transformer designs. HVT reduces sequence length through pooling, while LeViT optimizes the speed–accuracy trade-off for fast inference and reports being five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU around 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy. Those efficiency claims belong to modified or hybrid models and specific hardware; they do not imply that the original ViT has the same latency advantage, and FLOPs alone do not determine measured speed. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:a066cd8b17bb] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214]

Task-specific evidence further narrows applicability. PVT was designed as a convolution-free replacement for CNN backbones across classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation; its reported RetinaNet result is discussed in the experimental comparison rather than treated as a general property of transformers. ViT-CoMer similarly targets detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation with added convolutional multi-scale fusion and reports strong COCO and ADE20K results under its own frameworks and pretraining conditions. By contrast, ConvLLaVA uses ConvNeXt in a large multimodal model to compress high-resolution visual tokens, which addresses token redundancy in a specific vision-language pipeline rather than providing a direct image-classification comparison between original ViT and CNN backbones. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:82373423792e] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:b632e07740d1] [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:249f77d01bf9] Behavioral applicability also extends beyond aggregate accuracy. A controlled comparative study of ConvNets and ViTs with similar ImageNet accuracy and compute requirements finds differences in error types, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance, including across supervised and CLIP training paradigms. This means that two backbones with the same nominal ImageNet score may not be interchangeable for a specialized application. For the original ViT-versus-CNN question, the practical implication is that mechanism, pretraining, and downstream behavior must all be specified: CNNs provide strong built-in locality and hierarchy, plain ViT provides flexible global token mixing that benefits from scale, and hybrids or adapters are separate attempts to combine those properties. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

Experimental comparison rule. The experiments below keep the review's organizing choice—architecture, training data, task fit, and measured behavior—and separate matched comparisons from results obtained with different models, tasks, or pretraining. The strongest direct statements about original ViT versus CNNs are therefore limited to settings that name the same dataset, model scale, training corpus, and metric. Results from PVT, CvT, LeViT, HVT, or ViT-CoMer describe modified or hybrid transformers and can quantify the cost of adding CNN-like hierarchy, locality, or speed optimizations, but they do not rank the original ViT as though it had those modifications. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:82373423792e]

Image classification under different data scales is the pivotal original ViT–CNN comparison. The CvT paper summarizes ViT's empirical regime as follows: a pure Transformer over non-overlapping patch tokens can attain state-of-the-art performance relative to CNNs such as ResNets and EfficientNet when trained on sufficiently large data, including ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, but it remains below similarly sized CNN counterparts when trained on smaller datasets. This is a regime-dependent result rather than a universal winner: a ViT model pretrained on JFT-scale data and a ResNet trained only on ImageNet-1K are not in an apples-to-apples data setting, and neither result should be generalized across both regimes. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88]

CvT also provides a hybrid-transformer classification result that should not be mistaken for plain ViT. With ImageNet-22k pretraining and ImageNet-1k validation, CvT-W24 reached 87.7% top-1 accuracy; the paper reports that its convolutional token embedding, convolutional projection, and multi-stage design outperformed other Vision Transformers and ResNets on ImageNet-1k while using fewer parameters and lower FLOPs. The comparison supports the specific claim that inserting convolution and hierarchy improved that CvT family under its training and model configurations. It does not establish that the original ViT, without those convolutional components, beats the same ResNets under the same conditions. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:37:72d5be829727:claim:9fc9d95ec61d] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44]

The LeViT experiments target a different objective: fast inference rather than unconstrained classification accuracy. LeViT is a hybrid that adopts CNN-style decreasing-resolution activation maps and uses attention bias for positional information; near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, the authors report that it is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. Because the metric combines accuracy with measured CPU speed, the result is a speed/accuracy trade-off claim for LeViT and EfficientNet on the stated hardware. It is not a latency comparison between original ViT and generic CNN backbones, and it cannot be inferred from parameter count or FLOPs alone. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:11:195dc7dad451:claim:1bb0a94cb919] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1]

HVT addresses compute by progressively pooling visual tokens, analogous to CNN downsampling, rather than retaining ViT's full patch sequence throughout inference. On ImageNet and CIFAR-100 image classification, the authors report that HVT outperforms competitive baselines at comparable FLOPs and that average-pooled visual tokens were more discriminative than a single class token in their empirical study. This supports token pooling as a scaling and efficiency mechanism for a hierarchical transformer. It is not a matched result for original ViT versus a CNN, because HVT changes the token sequence and representation hierarchy rather than evaluating the unchanged ViT encoder. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56]

Dense-prediction results expose the clearest task-interface difference. PVT was explicitly built to overcome plain ViT's typically low-resolution output and high computational or memory cost by producing transformer feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32. In its reported COCO object-detection experiment, RetinaNet with PVT achieved 40.4 AP, surpassing RetinaNet with ResNet-50 at 36.3 AP by 4.1 absolute AP at a comparable parameter count. The paper also reports that PVT-Large reached 42.6 AP, 1.6 points above ResNeXt101-64x4d while using 30% fewer parameters. These are matched-task comparisons for PVT versus CNN backbones, but PVT is a pyramid transformer rather than original ViT. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce]

ViT-CoMer supplies later evidence that adding convolutional multi-scale features can improve a plain pretrained ViT for dense prediction. With Mask R-CNN on COCO val2017, the reported table includes ViT-S at 44.0% box AP with 44M parameters versus ViT-CoMer-S at 47.1% with 29M parameters, and ViT-B at 45.8% with 114M parameters versus ViT-CoMer-B at 50.2% with 129M parameters under ImageNet-1K pretraining. With advanced pretraining, marked by the dagger symbol, ViT-CoMer-S reached 52.1%, ViT-CoMer-B 54.2%, and ViT-CoMer-L 55.9% box AP; the paper separately reports ViT-CoMer-L at 64.3% AP under its broader detection setup and 62.1% mIoU on ADE20K validation. These values quantify gains from the added CNN–Transformer fusion, not standalone performance of the original ViT architecture. In the same Mask R-CNN table, InternImage-T reached 49.1% box AP with 49M parameters, ViT-Adapter-T reached 46.0% with 28M, and ViT-CoMer-T reached 47.1% with 29M; at base scale, InternImage-B reached 50.3% with 115M, ViT-Adapter-B reached 49.6% with 120M, and ViT-CoMer-B reached 50.2% with 129M. Representation experiments show that ViTs and ResNets differ even when they solve the same classification task. CKA heatmaps in the controlled analysis found that ViTs had a more uniform internal similarity structure, with greater similarity between lower and higher layers, while ResNet representations were more separated into stages. Cross-model CKA indicated that many lower ResNet layers corresponded to roughly the lowest quarter of ViT layers, and the upper half of ResNet corresponded approximately to the next third of ViT layers; the final third of ViT layers was less similar to ResNet representations. Attention-distance measurements over 5,000 data points further found local and global heads in early ViT layers and global heads at higher layers, unlike early CNN layers with fixed local receptive fields. These are behavioral measurements, not accuracy rankings. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:0d7a530b916e] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:b1420373012c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6d5dc789edf3] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:5_local_and_global_information_in_layer_representations:0:41d4ea1578cc:claim:39e9842ac6c6]

Broad backbone benchmarks and behavioral studies argue against selecting a backbone from one ImageNet number. Battle of the Backbones evaluated more than 1,500 runs across classification, detection, out-of-distribution settings and other tasks; within its included model and pretraining suite, supervised ConvNeXt, ImageNet-21k-trained SwinV2, and CLIP ViT-Base were highlighted as strong, while supervised CNNs trained on large datasets performed best on most considered tasks. The authors caution that pretraining-data scale explains part of that outcome and report ViTs to be more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. A separate matched-accuracy, matched-compute comparison finds that ConvNets and ViTs can differ in mistakes, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Thus the experimental conclusion is conditional: CNN backbones show strong built-in locality and dense-prediction compatibility, original ViT is most competitive at adequate scale, and modified transformer results cannot be used as unmatched proof that plain ViT dominates CNNs. ## Limitations and Open Problems

Open problems and trade-offs. The first unresolved issue is that architecture, pretraining corpus, and training recipe remain entangled in ViT–CNN comparisons. Plain ViT has fewer vision-specific inductive biases than CNNs, and the cited evidence consistently ties its strongest classification results to sufficiently large data, such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, or to alternative recipes such as distillation and strong regularization. Battle of the Backbones further reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and model size, while some apparent supervised-model advantages are confounded by larger training sets. The implication is that future comparisons must report data scale, supervision type, distillation teacher, augmentation, regularization, and model capacity together; otherwise a win may describe the training regime rather than the backbone. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5]

A second open problem is that ImageNet top-1 accuracy remains an insufficient selection criterion, even after controlling for compute. The Beyond-ImageNet analysis selected ConvNets and ViTs with similar ImageNet accuracy and compute requirements but still found differences in error types, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Battle of the Backbones likewise broadened evaluation to detection, out-of-distribution behavior, and other tasks across more than 1,500 runs. This means that practitioners cannot infer robustness, calibration, or downstream suitability from a single classification score. The open challenge is to establish standardized, task-relevant evaluation suites that distinguish representation quality from nominal accuracy and that avoid overgeneralizing from one benchmark distribution. [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:9b280ab2685b] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5]

Plain ViT's dense-prediction interface remains a concrete limitation. The original architecture processes a patch-token sequence for classification and typically lacks the staged, multi-scale feature maps that ResNet-like CNN backbones expose through strides and downsampling. PVT was created because ViT's low-resolution outputs and high computational or memory cost made it difficult to port directly to dense tasks; its pyramid outputs at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32 were needed to emulate a CNN backbone interface. ViT-CoMer similarly identifies limited inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity as reasons plain ViT underperforms in detection and segmentation. The trade-off is therefore not merely accuracy: using plain ViT for pixel-level tasks may require adapters, pyramids, convolutional features, or a redesigned detection head. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:82373423792e] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:b632e07740d1] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:4d1864524c5a]

High-resolution compute is a separate bottleneck. Standard self-attention over all patch tokens has quadratic complexity with respect to token count, and the dynamic-convolution analysis identifies that cost together with slower vanilla-ViT convergence as motivations for reintroducing CNN modules, feature pyramids, or local windows. PVT addresses dense feature maps with progressive shrinking, HVT pools tokens to shorten the sequence, and CvT uses convolutional token embedding and projection with a hierarchical design. These modifications show that the cost can be managed, but they also change the original ViT architecture. A remaining problem is to obtain global context and high-resolution localization without paying the full quadratic token-interaction cost or sacrificing the simplicity of plain ViT. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:a066cd8b17bb] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:644d231d8295] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88]

Position handling and variable-resolution deployment are not fully settled. The original ViT depends on positional encoding because self-attention is permutation invariant, whereas CNNs derive spatial structure from local grid operations. CvT reports that convolutional token embedding and convolutional projection introduce enough local spatial structure to remove positional encoding, which may simplify adaptation to higher-resolution vision tasks. That result is specific to CvT's hybrid design, however, and does not imply that original ViT position embeddings transfer seamlessly to arbitrary resolutions or downstream token layouts. Future work still needs to separate true spatial generalization from interpolation, resolution tuning, and architecture-specific effects. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:37:72d5be829727:claim:9fc9d95ec61d]

The internal-representation studies expose an explanatory gap rather than a complete design theory. CKA shows that ViTs maintain a more uniform representation structure across layers, while ResNets separate more clearly into stages; attention-distance measurements show local and global heads in early ViT layers and global heads in higher layers, unlike the fixed local receptive fields of early CNN layers. These observations explain why the models can behave differently even at similar accuracy, but they do not yet provide a universal rule for when global attention is preferable to staged convolution, or which representation property causes calibration, transfer, or robustness differences. More causal interventions are needed beyond measuring similarity or attention distance. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:0d7a530b916e] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:b1420373012c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6d5dc789edf3] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:5_local_and_global_information_in_layer_representations:0:41d4ea1578cc:claim:39e9842ac6c6]

Hybrid and hierarchical architectures demonstrate practical remedies but complicate the scientific comparison. PVT, HVT, CvT, LeViT, and ViT-CoMer each borrow some CNN-like property—pyramids, downsampling or pooling, convolutional tokenization/projection, decreasing-resolution maps, or convolutional multi-scale fusion—and report benefits for efficiency, classification, or dense prediction. Their success does not answer the narrower question of whether unchanged ViT is intrinsically better than a CNN; it shows that many strong vision systems occupy a middle design space. The open problem is to attribute gains accurately among locality, hierarchy, position encoding, token reduction, pretraining, and added parameters rather than labeling every improved transformer as evidence for or against the original ViT. Efficiency claims also remain hardware- and objective-dependent. LeViT's reported five-fold CPU speed advantage over EfficientNet near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy is a measured speed/accuracy result for that hybrid model and hardware, while HVT's comparable-FLOPs classification results do not by themselves establish latency. ED-ViT instead addresses edge deployment by splitting and pruning ViT models, reporting substantial model-size and latency reductions in its multi-device setting. Because parameters, FLOPs, peak memory, throughput, and latency measure different constraints, future backbone comparisons should report end-to-end inference on the target hardware and task. A model that is efficient for classification may still be expensive when adapted to high-resolution detection or multimodal token compression. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:b33d5ca4d495] [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:249f77d01bf9]

Dense-prediction evidence also shows that adding CNN-like structure can improve plain ViT, but at the cost of additional modules and training assumptions. ViT-CoMer uses a pretrained ViT while adding a spatial pyramid of convolutional features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion; its strongest results rely on advanced open-source pretraining, and the paper distinguishes ImageNet-1K rows from advanced-pretraining rows. PVT's COCO gains over ResNet-50 and ResNeXt101 come from a pyramid transformer rather than original ViT. Thus the remaining practical problem is not only how to improve dense prediction, but how to do so with controlled extra compute, clear pretraining conditions, and fair comparisons against modern CNNs under the same detection or segmentation framework. Finally, the field lacks a timeless winner because task constraints keep changing the appropriate backbone. CNNs retain strong built-in locality, translation-related structure, and hierarchical feature maps; plain ViT offers flexible global, input-dependent token mixing but requires adequate data and is less naturally matched to conventional multi-scale dense-prediction interfaces; hybrids and adapted ViTs narrow specific gaps but introduce their own assumptions. The cited benchmark and analysis papers support conditional conclusions rather than a universal ranking. Future progress should therefore use matched-data, matched-compute, task-specific, and hardware-specific evaluations, while reporting whether the evaluated system is a plain ViT, a conventional CNN, or a modified architecture that combines mechanisms from both families. ## Conclusion

There is no timeless winner between the original ViT and CNN backbones. CNNs are the stronger default when the desired interface is local, hierarchical, multi-scale feature extraction for detection or segmentation, and when training must rely on a relatively small corpus. Plain ViT is most compelling for classification when large-scale pretraining or a validated data-efficient recipe supplies the visual bias that the architecture does not hard-code. Its standard all-token attention also makes high-resolution use costly, and latency or edge suitability must be measured on the target system rather than inferred from FLOPs. The evidence favors matched, task-specific selection. A fair ViT–CNN comparison must name the exact backbone, parameter scale, dataset, pretraining, supervision, distillation teacher, augmentations, task metric, and hardware, while keeping plain ViT, conventional CNNs, and hybrid or hierarchical transformers as distinct evidence groups.
