## Limitations and Open Problems

Open problems and trade-offs. The first unresolved issue is that architecture, pretraining corpus, and training recipe remain entangled in ViT–CNN comparisons. Plain ViT has fewer vision-specific inductive biases than CNNs, and the cited evidence consistently ties its strongest classification results to sufficiently large data, such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, or to alternative recipes such as distillation and strong regularization. Battle of the Backbones further reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and model size, while some apparent supervised-model advantages are confounded by larger training sets. The implication is that future comparisons must report data scale, supervision type, distillation teacher, augmentation, regularization, and model capacity together; otherwise a win may describe the training regime rather than the backbone. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:8:4404c16be017:claim:52fda25edc44] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5]

A second open problem is that ImageNet top-1 accuracy remains an insufficient selection criterion, even after controlling for compute. The Beyond-ImageNet analysis selected ConvNets and ViTs with similar ImageNet accuracy and compute requirements but still found differences in error types, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Battle of the Backbones likewise broadened evaluation to detection, out-of-distribution behavior, and other tasks across more than 1,500 runs. This means that practitioners cannot infer robustness, calibration, or downstream suitability from a single classification score. The open challenge is to establish standardized, task-relevant evaluation suites that distinguish representation quality from nominal accuracy and that avoid overgeneralizing from one benchmark distribution. [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:9b280ab2685b] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5]

Plain ViT's dense-prediction interface remains a concrete limitation. The original architecture processes a patch-token sequence for classification and typically lacks the staged, multi-scale feature maps that ResNet-like CNN backbones expose through strides and downsampling. PVT was created because ViT's low-resolution outputs and high computational or memory cost made it difficult to port directly to dense tasks; its pyramid outputs at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32 were needed to emulate a CNN backbone interface. ViT-CoMer similarly identifies limited inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity as reasons plain ViT underperforms in detection and segmentation. The trade-off is therefore not merely accuracy: using plain ViT for pixel-level tasks may require adapters, pyramids, convolutional features, or a redesigned detection head. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:82373423792e] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:b632e07740d1] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:4d1864524c5a]

High-resolution compute is a separate bottleneck. Standard self-attention over all patch tokens has quadratic complexity with respect to token count, and the dynamic-convolution analysis identifies that cost together with slower vanilla-ViT convergence as motivations for reintroducing CNN modules, feature pyramids, or local windows. PVT addresses dense feature maps with progressive shrinking, HVT pools tokens to shorten the sequence, and CvT uses convolutional token embedding and projection with a hierarchical design. These modifications show that the cost can be managed, but they also change the original ViT architecture. A remaining problem is to obtain global context and high-resolution localization without paying the full quadratic token-interaction cost or sacrificing the simplicity of plain ViT. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:a066cd8b17bb] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:644d231d8295] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88]

Position handling and variable-resolution deployment are not fully settled. The original ViT depends on positional encoding because self-attention is permutation invariant, whereas CNNs derive spatial structure from local grid operations. CvT reports that convolutional token embedding and convolutional projection introduce enough local spatial structure to remove positional encoding, which may simplify adaptation to higher-resolution vision tasks. That result is specific to CvT's hybrid design, however, and does not imply that original ViT position embeddings transfer seamlessly to arbitrary resolutions or downstream token layouts. Future work still needs to separate true spatial generalization from interpolation, resolution tuning, and architecture-specific effects. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:section:abstract:8:72c672e9b982:claim:ce8ab5488cc1] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:1b8ce56ebfd9] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:37:72d5be829727:claim:9fc9d95ec61d]

The internal-representation studies expose an explanatory gap rather than a complete design theory. CKA shows that ViTs maintain a more uniform representation structure across layers, while ResNets separate more clearly into stages; attention-distance measurements show local and global heads in early ViT layers and global heads in higher layers, unlike the fixed local receptive fields of early CNN layers. These observations explain why the models can behave differently even at similar accuracy, but they do not yet provide a universal rule for when global attention is preferable to staged convolution, or which representation property causes calibration, transfer, or robustness differences. More causal interventions are needed beyond measuring similarity or attention distance. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:0d7a530b916e] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:b1420373012c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6d5dc789edf3] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:5_local_and_global_information_in_layer_representations:0:41d4ea1578cc:claim:39e9842ac6c6]

Hybrid and hierarchical architectures demonstrate practical remedies but complicate the scientific comparison. PVT, HVT, CvT, LeViT, and ViT-CoMer each borrow some CNN-like property—pyramids, downsampling or pooling, convolutional tokenization/projection, decreasing-resolution maps, or convolutional multi-scale fusion—and report benefits for efficiency, classification, or dense prediction. Their success does not answer the narrower question of whether unchanged ViT is intrinsically better than a CNN; it shows that many strong vision systems occupy a middle design space. The open problem is to attribute gains accurately among locality, hierarchy, position encoding, token reduction, pretraining, and added parameters rather than labeling every improved transformer as evidence for or against the original ViT. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:ea5eac42cf88] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:82373423792e] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:b632e07740d1]

Efficiency claims also remain hardware- and objective-dependent. LeViT's reported five-fold CPU speed advantage over EfficientNet near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy is a measured speed/accuracy result for that hybrid model and hardware, while HVT's comparable-FLOPs classification results do not by themselves establish latency. ED-ViT instead addresses edge deployment by splitting and pruning ViT models, reporting substantial model-size and latency reductions in its multi-device setting. Because parameters, FLOPs, peak memory, throughput, and latency measure different constraints, future backbone comparisons should report end-to-end inference on the target hardware and task. A model that is efficient for classification may still be expensive when adapted to high-resolution detection or multimodal token compression. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:62384841d214] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:b33d5ca4d495] [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:249f77d01bf9]

Dense-prediction evidence also shows that adding CNN-like structure can improve plain ViT, but at the cost of additional modules and training assumptions. ViT-CoMer uses a pretrained ViT while adding a spatial pyramid of convolutional features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion; its strongest results rely on advanced open-source pretraining, and the paper distinguishes ImageNet-1K rows from advanced-pretraining rows. PVT's COCO gains over ResNet-50 and ResNeXt101 come from a pyramid transformer rather than original ViT. Thus the remaining practical problem is not only how to improve dense prediction, but how to do so with controlled extra compute, clear pretraining conditions, and fair comparisons against modern CNNs under the same detection or segmentation framework. Finally, the field lacks a timeless winner because task constraints keep changing the appropriate backbone. CNNs retain strong built-in locality, translation-related structure, and hierarchical feature maps; plain ViT offers flexible global, input-dependent token mixing but requires adequate data and is less naturally matched to conventional multi-scale dense-prediction interfaces; hybrids and adapted ViTs narrow specific gaps but introduce their own assumptions. The cited benchmark and analysis papers support conditional conclusions rather than a universal ranking. Future progress should therefore use matched-data, matched-compute, task-specific, and hardware-specific evaluations, while reporting whether the evaluated system is a plain ViT, a conventional CNN, or a modified architecture that combines mechanisms from both families. ## Conclusion

There is no timeless winner between the original ViT and CNN backbones. CNNs are the stronger default when the desired interface is local, hierarchical, multi-scale feature extraction for detection or segmentation, and when training must rely on a relatively small corpus. Plain ViT is most compelling for classification when large-scale pretraining or a validated data-efficient recipe supplies the visual bias that the architecture does not hard-code. Its standard all-token attention also makes high-resolution use costly, and latency or edge suitability must be measured on the target system rather than inferred from FLOPs. The evidence favors matched, task-specific selection. Reported PVT detection gains, CvT's 87.7% ImageNet-22k-pretrained CvT-W24 top-1 result, LeViT's CPU speed/accuracy claim, HVT pooling results, and ViT-CoMer's COCO/ADE20K improvements show that hierarchy, convolution, pooling, and fusion can remedy plain-ViT limitations, but they evaluate changed architectures. A fair ViT–CNN comparison must name the exact backbone, parameter scale, dataset, pretraining, supervision, distillation teacher, augmentations, task metric, and hardware, while keeping plain ViT, conventional CNNs, and hybrid or hierarchical transformers as distinct evidence groups. claim_records.text: HIRI-ViT upgrades prevalent four-stage ViT to a five-stage ViT tailored for high-resolution inputs.
Under comparable computational cost of approximately 5.0 GFLOPs, HIRI-ViT achieves 84.3% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 448×448 inputs.
HIRI-ViT's 84.3% Top-1 accuracy with 448×448 inputs improves iFormer-S's 83.4% Top-1 accuracy with 224×224 inputs by 0.9%.
Experiments on recognition task (ImageNet-1K dataset) and dense prediction tasks (COCO and ADE20K datasets) demonstrate the superiority of HIRI-ViT.

HRViT and HRFormer target constructing Vision Transformer with multi-scale inputs by keeping all resolutions throughout the network and performing cross-resolution interaction, but their inputs are still limited to 224×224 resolution.

In HIRI-ViT, IRDS-a is adopted for downsampling in the first two stages with high resolution inputs: it first uses a strided 3×3 convolution to expand dimension and reduce spatial size, then a 1×1 convolution to shrink channel dimension.
In HIRI-ViT, IRDS-b is leveraged for the last two downsampling layers, similar to inverted residual block but only applies normalization and activation operations after the first convolution.
HIRI-ViT constructs three variants in different model sizes: HIRI-ViT-S (small size), HIRI-ViT-B (base size), and HIRI-ViT-L (large size).
The entire architecture of HIRI-ViT is composed of one HR-stem layer and five stages.
When directly enlarging the input resolution of Swin Transformer from 224×224 to 384×384, the top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K is evidently affected alongside sharply increased computational costs.

claim_records.text: CrossViT proposes a dual-branch transformer that processes small-patch and large-patch tokens with two separate branches of different computational complexity, fusing tokens purely by attention multiple times.

CrossViT's cross-attention token fusion module uses a single token for each branch as a query to exchange information with other branches, requiring only linear time for both computational and memory complexity instead of quadratic time.
On the ImageNet1K dataset, with some architectural changes, CrossViT outperforms DeiT by a large margin of 2% with a small to moderate increase in FLOPs and model parameters.
Vision Transformer (ViT) requires very large datasets such as ImageNet21K and JFT300M for training.
DeiT shows that data augmentation and model regularization can enable training of high-performance ViT models with fewer data.

CrossViT's approach performs better than or on par with several concurrent works based on ViT, and demonstrates comparable results with EfficientNet with regards to accuracy, throughput and model parameters.

BoTNet replaced the spatial convolutions with global self-attention in the final three bottleneck blocks of a ResNet, resulting in models that achieve strong performance for image classification on ImageNet benchmark.
T2T-ViT introduces a layer-wise Tokens-to-Token (T2T) transformation to encode important local structure for each token instead of the naive tokenization used in ViT.

claim_records.text: With a comparable number of parameters, RetinaNet+PVT achieves 40.4 AP on the COCO dataset, surpassing RetinaNet+ResNet50 (36.3 AP) by 4.1 absolute AP.
PVT-Large achieves 42.6 AP, which is 1.6 points better than ResNeXt101-64x4d, with 30% less parameters.

The entire PVT model is divided into four stages, each comprised of a patch embedding layer and a Li-layer Transformer encoder, with output resolution progressively shrinking from 4-stride to 32-stride following a pyramid structure.

PVT obtains feature maps F1, F2, F3, and F4 whose strides are 4, 8, 16, and 32 pixels with respect to the input image, enabling application to downstream tasks including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

claim_records.text: BoB benchmarks a diverse suite of pretrained models, including vision-language models, those trained via self-supervised learning, and the Stable Diffusion backbone, across computer vision tasks ranging from classification to object detection to OOD generalization.
The BoB comprehensive analysis was conducted on more than 1500 training runs.
Among the models considered in BoB, convolutional neural networks pretrained in a supervised fashion on large training sets still perform best on most tasks.
In apples-to-apples comparisons on the same architectures and similarly sized pretraining datasets, SSL backbones are highly competitive.

Across the BoB suite of evaluations spanning tasks, datasets, and settings including ID and OOD, supervised ConvNeXt-Base, supervised SwinV2-Base trained using ImageNet-21k, and CLIP ViT-Base come out on top.
Among smaller backbones, ConvNeXt-Tiny and SwinV2-Tiny emerge victorious, followed by DINO ViT-Small.
High-performance convolutional networks pretrained via supervised learning outperform transformers on the majority of tasks considered in BoB.

claim_records.text: Vision Transformers can be interpreted as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions, enabling existing Transformers and dynamic ConvNets to be characterized in a unified framework.
Replacing the softmax activation in vision Transformers with commonly used ConvNet modules such as ReLU and Layer Normalization results in a faster convergence rate and better performance.
A depth-wise vision Transformer created following depth-wise convolution design is more efficient with comparable performance.

fact_fields.method: architectural redesign following depth-wise convolution principles

claim_records.text: The query-key and attention-value matrix multiplications in a standard self-attention block can be interpreted as two 1×1 dynamic convolutions, with the scaled softmax operation treated as an activation function.
Replacing softmax with LayerNorm and ReLU in Swin-Tiny, without introducing any computational cost, improves top-1 ImageNet accuracy from 81.13 to 81.56.
Being S-shaped is a downside of softmax because it slows down the convergence rate compared to non-S-shaped functions such as ReLU.
Non-linearity and normalization play more important parts in softmax's role in Transformers than its S-shaped property, and can be substituted by techniques other than softmax.

fact_fields.method: ablation study of softmax functional roles

claim_records.text: The dynamic convolution kernels generated from one spatial location in self-attention are shared with other locations through a global kernel bank, which is more efficient than generating a new set of kernels for each spatial location.

fact_fields.method: architectural analysis of self-attention dynamic convolution mechanism

claim_records.text: The vanilla ViT has quadratic computational complexity with respect to input resolution, making it prohibitive to serve as a general backbone for computer vision tasks.
Vision Transformers implicitly approximate a dense kernel with a pair of lightweight kernels, which is a unique efficiency design not present in existing dynamic convolution approaches.

claim_records.text: Analyzing internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks reveals striking differences between the two architectures, including ViT having more uniform representations across all layers.
Self-attention plays a crucial role in enabling early aggregation of global information in ViTs, contributing to observed representation differences from CNNs.
ViT residual connections strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers, contributing to the uniform representation structure of ViTs.
ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods on spatial localization.

Using CKA to compute pairwise layer similarity within models, ViTs show a much more uniform similarity structure with a clear grid-like structure, while ResNets have similarity divided into different lower/higher stages.

fact_fields.method: Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) pairwise layer similarity computation

claim_records.text: Lower and higher layers in ViT show much greater similarity than in ResNet, where similarity is divided into different lower/higher stages.

fact_fields.method: Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) pairwise layer similarity computation

claim_records.text: In cross-model CKA comparisons, the lower half of 60 ResNet layers are similar to approximately the lowest quarter of ViT layers.
In cross-model CKA comparisons, the top half of the ResNet is approximately similar to the next third of the ViT layers.

Even in the lowest layers of ViT, self-attention layers have a mix of local heads (small distances) and global heads (large distances), in contrast to CNNs which are hardcoded to attend only locally in lower layers.

fact_fields.method: self-attention distance analysis: weighting pixel distances by attention weights per head, averaged over datapoints

claim_records.text: At higher ViT layers, all self-attention heads are global.

claim_records.text: ViT effective receptive fields shift from local to global, while ResNet effective receptive fields are highly local and grow gradually.

fact_fields.method: effective receptive field measurement: absolute value of gradient of center feature map location (after residual connections) with respect to input, averaged across channels

claim_records.text: Most information in ViT passes through skip connections, with a clear phase transition from preserving the CLS (class) token representation in lower layers to spatial token representations in higher layers.

fact_fields.method: comparison of representation norms between skip-connection (identity) branch and long branch

claim_records.text: PiT outperforms the ViT baseline across image classification, object detection, and robustness evaluation tasks.

Modern CNN architectures including AlexNet, ResNet, and EfficientNet follow the design principle of gradually increasing channel size while decreasing spatial size as depth increases.

fact_fields.method: Review of CNN architectural design conventions

claim_records.text: Experiments show that ResNet-style dimension configurations improve the model capability and generalization performance of ResNet.

claim_records.text: PiT incorporates a newly designed pooling layer that enables spatial size reduction in the ViT structure, matching the dimension progression used in ResNet.

claim_records.text: AlexNet uses three max-pooling layers, each reducing feature spatial size by half, with channel size increased by subsequent convolution after pooling.
VGGnet uses 5 spatial resolutions via 5 max-pooling layers, each reducing spatial size by half and doubling channel size.
ResNet performs spatial size reduction using stride-2 convolution layers instead of max pooling, an improvement over prior spatial reduction methods.

Funnel Transformer improves transformer architecture performance by reducing tokens via a pooling layer and skip-connection, but its pooling application method differs from PiT due to fundamental architectural differences between NLP and computer vision.

fact_fields.method: Comparative review of Funnel Transformer and PiT pooling approaches

claim_records.text: Most convolution networks use a dimension configuration with spatial reduction, as reported in prior work including ReXNet which found channel configuration significantly impacts network performance.

fact_fields.method: Review of prior convolution network design studies

Prior works that replace 3×3 convolution with self-attention or add self-attention layers inherit the basic ResNet structure, including stride-2 convolution layers that preserve ResNet's dimension configuration.

claim_records.text: ViT-ResNAS is an efficient multi-stage ViT architecture designed with neural architecture search, incorporating residual spatial reduction and weight-sharing NAS with multi-architectural sampling.

fact_fields.method: Neural architecture search for multi-stage ViT design

claim_records.text: Residual spatial reduction decreases sequence lengths for deeper layers in a multi-stage architecture, with added skip connections to improve performance and stabilize training of deeper networks.

Weight-sharing NAS with multi-architectural sampling trains a super-network covering all sub-networks by sampling and training multiple sub-networks in one forward-backward pass, followed by evolutionary search to discover high-performance architectures.
On ImageNet, ViT-ResNAS achieves better accuracy-MACs and accuracy-throughput trade-offs than the original DeiT and other strong ViT baselines.

The ViT-ResNAS search space is defined by sub-networks with smaller depths and widths contained within an enlarged ViT-Res network; for each stage, embedding dimension and number of transformer blocks are searched, and for each block, number of attention heads in MHSA and hidden size in FFN are searched.
The super-network for weight-sharing NAS has the same architecture as the largest network defining the search space, with weights shared across all sub-networks.

After super-network training, evolutionary search is applied to discover high-performance sub-networks satisfying resource constraints such as MACs, and the best evaluated sub-network is trained from scratch.
ViT demonstrates that a pure transformer without convolution can achieve impressive image classification performance when trained on large datasets such as JFT-300M.
DeiT shows that ViT can outperform CNN when trained on ImageNet with stronger regularization.

Weight-sharing NAS accelerates architecture search by training a single super-network whose weights are shared across all networks in the search space, allowing direct approximation of sub-network performance without training each network from scratch.
Self-attention and Transformers originating from NLP have been widely adopted in computer vision tasks including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

fact_fields.method: Review of Transformer applications in computer vision

claim_records.text: Pioneering NAS works use reinforcement learning to sample many networks in a pre-defined search space and train them from scratch for a few epochs to approximate performance, which requires expensive computation.

claim_records.text: Vision Transformers (ViT) are competitive with convnets but have not yet delivered clear benefits over them: they are computationally more demanding, require more training data, and their features do not exhibit unique properties.
The ViT architecture takes as input a grid of non-overlapping contiguous image patches of resolution N × N, typically using N = 16 ("/16") or N = 8 ("/8").
The DINO projection head consists of a 3-layer MLP with hidden dimension 2048 followed by l2 normalization and a weight normalized fully connected layer with K dimensions.
When applying DINO to ViT, no batch normalization is used in the projection heads, making the system entirely BN-free.

claim_records.text: A pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches performs very well on image classification tasks, removing the necessity of relying on convolutional neural networks.

When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and VTAB benchmarks, ViT attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

The Vision Transformer reshapes an input 2D image into a sequence of flattened 2D patches, maps these patches to constant latent vector size D via a trainable linear projection, and prepends a learnable class token whose final encoder state serves as the image representation.

Vision Transformer matches or exceeds the state of the art on many image classification datasets while being relatively cheap to pre-train, with no image-specific inductive biases introduced apart from the initial patch extraction step.

Prior vision models combining CNN-like architectures with self-attention, including those replacing convolutions entirely, have not been scaled effectively on modern hardware accelerators due to specialized attention patterns, leaving classic ResNet-like architectures as the state of the art in large-scale image recognition.

fact_fields.method: Prior CNN-self-attention hybrid and convolution-free vision models

claim_records.text: Vision Transformers dominate ResNets on the performance/compute trade-off, using approximately 2-4× less compute to attain the same performance averaged over 5 datasets.
Hybrid ResNet-ViT models slightly outperform pure ViT at small computational budgets, but this performance difference vanishes for larger models.

fact_fields.method: Hybrid ResNet-ViT vs pure ViT comparison

claim_records.text: Vision Transformers do not show performance saturation within the tested pre-training compute range, motivating future scaling efforts.

claim_records.text: Vision Transformers' inherent reliance on sequential input enforces manual partitioning of images into patch sequences, which disrupts the image's inherent structural and semantic continuity.
Pattern Transformer (Patternformer) adaptively converts images to pattern sequences for Transformer input.

Patternformer employs a Convolutional Neural Network to extract various patterns from the input image, with each channel representing a unique pattern fed into the succeeding Transformer as a visual token.
By enabling the network to optimize these patterns, each pattern concentrates on its local region of interest, thereby preserving its intrinsic structural and semantic information.
Using only vanilla ResNet and Transformer, Patternformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

claim_records.text: Swin Transformer achieves 87.3 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K for image classification.
Swin Transformer achieves 58.7 box AP and 51.1 mask AP on COCO test-dev for object detection.
Swin Transformer achieves 53.5 mIoU on ADE20K val for semantic segmentation.
The shifted windowing scheme of Swin Transformer brings greater efficiency by limiting self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows while also allowing for cross-window connection.
The hierarchical architecture of Swin Transformer has the flexibility to model at various scales and has linear computational complexity with respect to image size.
Swin Transformer's performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by +2.7 box AP and +2.6 mask AP on COCO.
Swin Transformer's performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by +3.2 mIoU on ADE20K.
The hierarchical design and shifted window approach of Swin Transformer also prove beneficial for all-MLP architectures.
Existing Transformer-based models produce feature maps of a single low resolution and have quadratic computation complexity to input image size due to computation of self-attention globally.

Swin Transformer builds hierarchical feature maps by merging image patches in deeper layers and has linear computation complexity to input image size due to computation of self-attention only within each local window.
Dense prediction tasks at the pixel level on high-resolution images would be intractable for standard Transformer as the computational complexity of its self-attention is quadratic to image size.

Unlike word tokens in language Transformers, visual elements can vary substantially in scale, making fixed-scale token property of existing Transformer-based models unsuitable for many vision applications.

CNNs and their variants are still the primary backbone architectures for computer vision applications, and Transformer-like architectures have strong potential for unified modeling between vision and language.

claim_records.text: ConvNeXt, a family of pure ConvNet models constructed entirely from standard ConvNet modules, achieves 87.8% ImageNet top-1 accuracy.
ConvNeXt outperforms Swin Transformers on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation tasks.
ConvNeXt maintains the simplicity and efficiency of standard ConvNets while competing favorably with Transformers in terms of accuracy and scalability.
Vision Transformers (ViTs) quickly superseded ConvNets as the state-of-the-art image classification model at the start of the "Roaring 20s" of visual recognition.
A vanilla ViT faces difficulties when applied to general computer vision tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.

Hierarchical Transformers such as Swin Transformers reintroduced several ConvNet priors, making Transformers practically viable as a generic vision backbone and demonstrating remarkable performance on a wide variety of vision tasks.
The effectiveness of hybrid ConvNet-Transformer approaches was largely credited to the intrinsic superiority of Transformers rather than the inherent inductive biases of convolutions.

Gradually "modernizing" a standard ResNet toward the design of a vision Transformer led to the discovery of several key components that contribute to performance differences, resulting in the ConvNeXt family of pure ConvNet models.

fact_fields.method: Gradually modernizing a standard ResNet toward vision Transformer design

claim_records.text: Except for the initial "patchify" layer that splits an image into a sequence of patches, ViT introduces no image-specific inductive bias and makes minimal changes to the original NLP Transformers.
With the help of larger model and dataset sizes, Transformers can outperform standard ResNets by a significant margin on image classification tasks.
ConvNeXt-T outperforms Swin-T on ImageNet-1K classification in the tested compute regime, significantly exceeding Swin-T's 81.3% top-1 accuracy.

The ConvNeXt model has approximately the same FLOPs, parameter count, throughput, and memory use as the Swin Transformer, but does not require specialized modules such as shifted window attention or relative position biases.

All design choices used to develop ConvNeXt are adapted from vision Transformers, and these designs are not novel even in the ConvNet literature as they have all been researched separately over the last decade.
The inference throughputs of ConvNeXts are comparable to or exceed that of Swin Transformers for both classification and other tasks requiring higher-resolution inputs.
Training ConvNeXts requires less memory than training Swin Transformers.
Training Cascade Mask-RCNN using ConvNeXt-B backbone consumes 17.4GB of peak memory with a per-GPU batch size of 2, while the reference number for Swin-B is 18.5GB.
Both ConvNeXt and Swin Transformer exhibit a more favorable accuracy-FLOPs trade-off than vanilla ViT due to local computations.
ConvNeXt-XL achieves an accuracy of 87.8%, a decent improvement over ConvNeXt-L at 384², demonstrating that ConvNeXts are scalable architectures.
With ImageNet-22K pre-training, ConvNeXt is able to outperform EfficientNetV2, further demonstrating the importance of large-scale training.

claim_records.text: The reference vision transformer with 86M parameters achieves top-1 accuracy of 83.1% (single-crop evaluation) on ImageNet with no external data.
Competitive convolution-free transformers can be trained on a single computer in less than 3 days using only ImageNet.
A teacher-student strategy specific to transformers relies on a distillation token ensuring that the student learns from the teacher through attention.
Token-based distillation with a convnet as teacher yields results competitive with convnets on ImageNet, reaching up to 85.2% accuracy.
DeiT models learned on a single node with 4 GPUs in three days achieve competitive results against the state of the art on ImageNet with no external data.
The distillation token-based procedure outperforms vanilla distillation by a significant margin.
With distillation, image transformers learn more from a convnet than from another transformer with comparable performance.
DeiT shows a major improvement of +6.3% top-1 accuracy in a comparable setting over previous ViT models trained on Imagenet1k only.
DeiT⚗, produced by distillation from a relatively weaker RegNetY, outperforms EfficientNet.
DeiT⚗ outperforms the ViT-B model pre-trained on JFT300M at resolution 384 by 1% top-1 accuracy (85.2% vs 84.15%), while being significantly faster to train.

DeiT is slightly below EfficientNet on the tradeoff between throughput and top-1 classification accuracy on ImageNet, showing vision transformers have almost closed the gap with convnets when training with ImageNet only.

claim_records.text: S2AFormer is an efficient Vision Transformer architecture featuring novel Strip Self-Attention (SSA).
S2AFormer includes Hybrid Perception Blocks (HPBs) designed to integrate the local perception capabilities of CNNs with the global context modeling of Transformer's attention mechanisms.
A key innovation of SSA is reducing the spatial dimensions of K and V while compressing the channel dimensions of Q and K.
The SSA design significantly reduces computational overhead while preserving accuracy, striking an optimal balance between efficiency and effectiveness.
S2AFormer is evaluated on ImageNet-1k for image classification, ADE20k for semantic segmentation, and COCO for object detection and instance segmentation.
S2AFormer achieves significant accuracy gains with superior efficiency in both GPU and non-GPU environments.

claim_records.text: A Vision Transformer (ViT) is a simple neural architecture amenable to serve several computer vision tasks.
ViTs have limited built-in architectural priors, in contrast to more recent architectures that incorporate priors either about the input data or of specific tasks.
Recent works show that ViTs benefit from self-supervised pre-training, in particular BerT-like pre-training like BeiT.
The paper revisits the supervised training of ViTs with a procedure that builds upon and simplifies a recipe introduced for training ResNet-50.
The supervised training procedure includes a new simple data-augmentation procedure with only 3 augmentations, closer to the practice in self-supervised learning.

Evaluations on image classification (ImageNet-1k with and without pre-training on ImageNet-21k), transfer learning and semantic segmentation show that the procedure outperforms by a large margin previous fully supervised training recipes for ViT.
The performance of the ViT trained with supervision is comparable to that of more recent architectures.
The results could serve as better baselines for recent self-supervised approaches demonstrated on ViT.

claim_records.text: HTR-ConvText integrates a residual Convolutional Neural Network backbone with a MobileViT with Positional Encoding block in its feature extraction stage to capture structural patterns and subtle writing details.
The ConvText encoder is a hybrid architecture combining global context and local features within a hierarchical structure that reduces sequence length for improved efficiency.
An auxiliary module in HTR-ConvText injects textual context to mitigate the weakness of Connectionist Temporal Classification.

Evaluations on IAM, READ2016, LAM and HANDS-VNOnDB demonstrate that HTR-ConvText achieves improved performance and better generalization compared to existing methods, especially in scenarios with limited training samples and high handwriting diversity.

claim_records.text: Modern neural network representations underpinning vision systems are subject to supervision collapse, whereby they lose any information that is not necessary for performing the training task, including information that may be necessary for transfer to new tasks or domains.
Self-supervised learning is employed as a method to encourage general-purpose features that transfer better, mitigating supervision collapse.

CrossTransformers, a novel Transformer based neural network architecture, can take a small number of labeled images and an unlabeled query, find coarse spatial correspondence between the query and the labeled images, and then infer class membership by computing distances between spatially-corresponding features.

The CrossTransformers-based classifier is more robust to task and domain shift, demonstrated via state-of-the-art performance on Meta-Dataset, a recent dataset for evaluating transfer from ImageNet to many other vision datasets.

claim_records.text: The feature maps of vision encoders are fundamental to myriad modern AI tasks, ranging from core perception algorithms (e.g. semantic segmentation, object detection, depth perception, etc.) to modern multimodal understanding in vision-language models (VLMs).
The frontier of general purpose vision backbones in computer vision is Vision Transformers (ViT), typically trained using contrastive loss (e.g. CLIP).
Most off-the-shelf ViTs, particularly CLIP, run at 224 times 224px resolution, while the "high-resolution" versions are around 378-448px, but still inflexible.

A novel method is introduced to coherently and cheaply upsample the feature maps of low-resolution vision encoders while picking up on fine-grained details that would otherwise be lost due to resolution.
The effectiveness of the upsampling approach is demonstrated on core perception tasks as well as within agglomerative model training using RADIO as a way of providing richer targets for distillation.

claim_records.text: Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) introduces less than 1% of model parameters as trainable parameters in the input space while keeping the model backbone frozen.
VPT outperforms full fine-tuning in many cases across model capacities and training data scales, while reducing per-task storage cost.
VPT applied to ConvNeXt-B (pre-trained on ImageNet-21k) outperforms full fine-tuning on 8 out of 19 VTAB-1k tasks.
VPT applied to ResNet-50 (pre-trained on ImageNet-1k) has no clear winner across all 19 VTAB-1k tasks.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, VPT-deep achieves 42.11 mIoU under single-scale inference.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, VPT-deep achieves 44.06 mIoU under multi-scale inference.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, VPT+Bias achieves 44.04 mIoU under single-scale inference.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, VPT+Bias achieves 45.63 mIoU under multi-scale inference.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, full fine-tuning achieves 48.31 mIoU under single-scale inference.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, full fine-tuning achieves 50.07 mIoU under multi-scale inference.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, VPT-deep has 13.43M tunable parameters.
On ADE20k semantic segmentation with SETR on ViT-L, full fine-tuning has 318.31M tunable parameters.
ViT-Huge has 632M parameters, while ResNet-50 has 25M parameters.
VPT-deep improves performance compared to VPT-shallow, which only inserts prompts for the first layer's input.
Full fine-tuning requires storing and deploying a separate copy of the backbone parameters for every single task.

claim_records.text: Mask3D is a self-supervised pre-training approach that leverages existing large-scale RGB-D data to embed 3D priors into 2D learned feature representations.
Mask3D formulates a pre-text reconstruction task by masking RGB and depth patches in individual RGB-D frames, without requiring 3D reconstructions or multi-view correspondences.
Mask3D notably outperforms existing self-supervised 3D pre-training approaches on ScanNet, NYUv2, and Cityscapes image understanding tasks.
Mask3D achieves an improvement of +6.5% mIoU against the state-of-the-art Pri3D on ScanNet image semantic segmentation.

claim_records.text: ViT achieves inferior performance to CNNs when trained from scratch on a midsize dataset like ImageNet.
The simple tokenization of input images in ViT fails to model important local structure such as edges and lines among neighboring pixels, leading to low training sample efficiency.
The redundant attention backbone design of ViT leads to limited feature richness for fixed computation budgets and limited training samples.

T2T-ViT incorporates a layer-wise Tokens-to-Token (T2T) transformation that progressively structurizes images to tokens by recursively aggregating neighboring tokens into one token, enabling local structure modeling and token length reduction.

fact_fields.method: Tokens-To-Token Vision Transformer (T2T-ViT) with layer-wise T2T transformation

claim_records.text: T2T-ViT reduces the parameter count and MACs of vanilla ViT by half while achieving more than 3.0% improvement when trained from scratch on ImageNet.
T2T-ViT with comparable size to ResNet50 (21.5M parameters) achieves 83.3% top1 accuracy at image resolution 384×384 on ImageNet.
T2T-ViT outperforms ResNets and achieves comparable performance with MobileNets by directly training on ImageNet.

Five CNN-derived architecture designs were explored for the ViT backbone: Dense connection as DenseNet, deep-narrow vs shallow-wide structure as in Wide-ResNets, channel attention as Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks, more split heads in multi-head attention as ResNeXt, and Ghost operations as GhostNet.

Among the explored CNN-derived architecture designs, the deep-narrow structure is the most efficient and effective for ViT, reducing parameter count and MACs significantly with nearly no degradation in performance.
T2T-ViT-14, T2T-ViT-19 and T2T-ViT-24 are designed to have comparable parameters with ResNet50, ResNet101 and ResNet152 respectively.

T2T-ViT-7 and T2T-ViT-12 are lite models with comparable model size to MobileNetV1 and MobileNetV2, achieved by reducing layer depth, hidden dimension, and MLP ratio without special efficient convolution designs.
Visual transformers with T2T module and efficient backbone can outperform CNNs at different complexities on ImageNet without pre-training on JFT-300M.

claim_records.text: The proposed Dual Path Network (DPN) shares common features while maintaining flexibility to explore new features through dual path architectures, combining benefits from both ResNet and DenseNet path topologies.
On the ImageNet-1k dataset, a shallow DPN surpasses the best ResNeXt-101(64x4d) with 26% smaller model size, 25% less computational cost and 8% lower memory consumption.
DPN-131 further pushes the state-of-the-art single model performance on ImageNet-1k with about 2 times faster training speed.
DPN demonstrates consistently better performance than DenseNet, ResNet and ResNeXt on Places365 scene classification, PASCAL VOC detection, and PASCAL VOC segmentation tasks.

claim_records.text: DiT is a self-supervised pre-trained Document Image Transformer model trained using large-scale unlabeled text images for Document AI tasks.

DiT can be leveraged as the backbone network for a variety of vision-based Document AI tasks including document image classification, document layout analysis, table detection, and text detection for OCR.
Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a document image classification performance improvement from 91.11 to 92.69 on the evaluated downstream task.
Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a document layout analysis performance improvement from 91.0 to 94.9 on the evaluated downstream task.
Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a table detection performance improvement from 94.23 to 96.55 on the evaluated downstream task.
Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a text detection for OCR performance improvement from 93.07 to 94.29 on the evaluated downstream task.

Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a document image classification performance improvement from 91.11 to 92.69 on the evaluated downstream task.
Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a document layout analysis performance improvement from 91.0 to 94.9 on the evaluated downstream task.
Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a table detection performance improvement from 94.23 to 96.55 on the evaluated downstream task.
Self-supervised pre-trained DiT achieves a text detection for OCR performance improvement from 93.07 to 94.29 on the evaluated downstream task.

claim_records.text: CBNetV2 is a backbone framework that groups multiple identical backbones connected through composite connections, integrating high- and low-level features of multiple backbone networks to gradually expand the receptive field for object detection.
CBNetV2 can be adapted to various backbones (CNN-based vs. Transformer-based) and head designs of most mainstream detectors (one-stage vs. two-stage, anchor-based vs. anchor-free-based).
Dual-Swin-L built with CBNetV2 achieves 59.4% box AP and 51.6% mask AP on COCO test-dev under the single-model and single-scale testing protocol.
Swin-L achieves 57.7% box AP and 50.2% mask AP on COCO test-dev as the prior state-of-the-art result.
With multi-scale testing, the CBNetV2-based single model achieves 60.1% box AP and 52.3% mask AP on COCO test-dev without using extra training data.
CBNetV2 introduces a more efficient, effective, and resource-friendly way to build high-performance backbone networks compared to simply increasing the depth and width of the network.

assertions.source_quote: This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with CNN backbones by architecture, data regime, task fit, and measured behavior. CNNs encode locality through shared sliding kernels and usually build hierarchical, multi-scale feature maps; plain ViT embeds non-overlapping patches and mixes tokens with global, content-dependent self-attention. The key empirical boundary is data scale: pure ViT can match or exceed CNNs such as ResNets and EfficientNet after ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M-scale pretraining, but may lag similarly sized CNNs on smaller data. Dense prediction is another boundary: original ViT is a patch-sequence classifier, whereas CNN backbones naturally expose pyramids. PVT, CvT, LeViT, HVT, and ViT-CoMer results therefore concern modified or hybrid designs, not unchanged ViT. assertions.source_quote: Measured evidence supports conditional conclusions. CKA and attention-distance analyses show different representation propagation: ViTs have relatively uniform layer similarity and mixed local/global heads even early, while ResNets separate more strongly into stages and early CNN layers have fixed local receptive fields. Models with similar ImageNet accuracy can also differ in errors, calibration, transfer, invariance, and out-of-distribution behavior. Battle of the Backbones ties some supervised-CNN strength to larger datasets and describes ViTs as more sensitive to pretraining amount and parameter count. Thus the trade-off is between CNNs’ built-in locality and dense-prediction compatibility and ViT’s flexible global mixing, whose strongest results depend on scale, regularization, distillation, or downstream adaptation. assertions.source_quote: The practical problem is backbone selection. A backbone is a pretrained or randomly initialized feature extractor used to build computer-vision systems, and for many years the default was an ImageNet-trained convolutional network. ViT changed this design space by applying a standard Transformer encoder to image patches, but its comparison with CNNs depends strongly on pretraining scale, model size, target task, and evaluation protocol. Battle of the Backbones makes this caution explicit: ImageNet classification alone does not determine which backbone is preferable across detection, out-of-distribution generalization, and other settings. assertions.source_quote: The central architectural contrast is between convolution's built-in local processing and ViT's global content-dependent attention. CNNs share convolutional kernels over the image and build visual context through local receptive fields; ViT instead splits an image into fixed-length, non-overlapping patch tokens and applies multi-head self-attention followed by position-wise feed-forward layers. This gives ViT fewer vision-specific inductive biases than CNNs, which can aid flexibility at large scale but also creates a greater need for data or regularization. CvT's authors summarize the original empirical boundary in similar terms: pure Transformers can match or exceed ResNets and EfficientNet when trained on sufficiently large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, while ViT under similarly sized CNNs can lag when trained on smaller data. This gives ViT fewer vision-specific inductive biases than CNNs, which can aid flexibility at large scale but also creates a greater need for data or regularization. CvT's authors summarize the original empirical boundary in similar terms: pure Transformers can match or exceed ResNets and EfficientNet when trained on sufficiently large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, while ViT under similarly sized CNNs can lag when trained on smaller data. assertions.source_quote: The comparison also cannot be reduced to classification-only performance. Plain ViT was designed primarily around a single patch sequence for classification, whereas CNN backbones commonly provide hierarchical, multi-scale feature maps useful for detection and segmentation. Later transformer work such as PVT introduced progressive shrinking and pyramid outputs specifically to make a convolution-free backbone usable for dense prediction; ViT-CoMer similarly attributes plain ViT's weak dense-prediction fit to limited inner-patch/local interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. These later systems are evidence of the original backbone's task boundary, not evidence that the original ViT itself already possessed those CNN-like pyramid properties. assertions.source_quote: Classification criteria for this review. This taxonomy organizes backbones by four linked comparison dimensions: feature locality and receptive-field growth, token or feature-map hierarchy, dependence on position encoding and pretraining, and suitability for classification versus dense prediction. These are review criteria for comparing the original ViT with CNN backbones, not a universal architecture taxonomy. They also do not equate model quality with inference efficiency: FLOPs, parameters, latency, hardware speed, memory, and edge-device deployment are related engineering dimensions, but each must be measured under its own setting. assertions.source_quote: At the architectural pole, a standard CNN backbone is a local, weight-sharing feature extractor: convolutional kernels slide over the image, encode nearby spatial structure as an inductive bias, and typically expand receptive field through depth and downsampling. A plain ViT is a global, content-dependent sequence model: fixed non-overlapping image patches become tokens, and self-attention can relate distant token positions in every layer. CKA-based analysis supports treating these as functionally different representations rather than merely different parameterizations: ViTs show a comparatively uniform similarity structure across lower and higher layers, whereas ResNets separate representations more strongly into stages. assertions.source_quote: The locality criterion should not be read as “CNN local, ViT global at every head.” Measurements of ViT attention distance find a mixture of local and global heads even in the lowest self-attention layers, with higher layers becoming global; by contrast, early CNN layers have fixed local receptive fields. This distinction matters because it describes the mechanism by which context is aggregated, not the final accuracy. A later unified interpretation goes further and analyzes vision Transformers as input-conditioned, dynamic convolutions, but that analysis is a bridge between design spaces; it does not make the original ViT operationally identical to a fixed-kernel CNN backbone. assertions.source_quote: The third axis is how spatial order and vision bias are supplied. The original ViT requires positional information because self-attention over a set is otherwise permutation invariant, while CNNs obtain spatial structure from local grid operations. Hybrid designs blur this boundary: CvT uses overlapping convolutional token embedding and convolutional projection in a multi-stage transformer and reports that positional encoding can be removed; LeViT borrows decreasing-resolution activation maps from CNNs and introduces attention bias for positional information. These are useful intermediate classes, but their results cannot be assigned to the original ViT or to pure CNNs without noting the hybrid mechanism. assertions.source_quote: Plain ViT mechanism. The original Vision Transformer treats image classification as sequence processing: an image is divided into fixed, non-overlapping patches, each patch is linearly embedded as a token, positional information is added, and repeated standard Transformer blocks use multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward networks to model relations among tokens. Its central contribution is not merely replacing convolution with attention, but showing that a pure Transformer encoder can be competitive with strong CNNs when visual training is conducted at sufficient scale. This applicability boundary is important: the architecture has comparatively few hand-designed vision biases, so its strongest case depends on large-scale pretraining or an alternative data-efficient training recipe rather than on convolution-like locality being built into every block. assertions.explanation: The CvT context explicitly states that ViT first proved a pure Transformer architecture can attain state-of-the-art performance when data is large enough.

assertions.source_quote: Plain ViT mechanism. The original Vision Transformer treats image classification as sequence processing: an image is divided into fixed, non-overlapping patches, each patch is linearly embedded as a token, positional information is added, and repeated standard Transformer blocks use multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward networks to model relations among tokens. Its central contribution is not merely replacing convolution with attention, but showing that a pure Transformer encoder can be competitive with strong CNNs when visual training is conducted at sufficient scale. This applicability boundary is important: the architecture has comparatively few hand-designed vision biases, so its strongest case depends on large-scale pretraining or an alternative data-efficient training recipe rather than on convolution-like locality being built into every block. assertions.source_quote: ViT's global aggregation differs from the staged processing of CNN backbones. In self-attention, each token can form input-dependent interactions with tokens across the image; empirical attention-distance analysis finds both local and global attention heads in the lowest ViT layers and global heads at higher layers. This gives plain ViT a direct route to long-range context, but it also means that locality, translation structure, and scale hierarchy are not imposed in the same explicit way as in a convolutional stack. The mechanism should therefore be interpreted as flexible, content-dependent mixing over a patch grid, not as a universal guarantee of better accuracy or efficiency. assertions.source_quote: Representation evidence reinforces that ViT and ResNet-style CNNs process visual information differently. Centered kernel alignment comparisons show that ViTs have a relatively uniform internal representation structure, with greater similarity between lower and higher layers, whereas ResNet representations separate more clearly into lower and higher stages. In cross-model comparisons, many lower ResNet layers were needed to approximate representations found in a smaller portion of the lower ViT, while later portions of the two models mapped less directly. These findings support a functional distinction in representation propagation; they do not by themselves establish that one architecture produces universally superior features. assertions.source_quote: CNN backbone mechanism. Conventional CNN backbones use shared convolutional kernels that slide over a two-dimensional image, giving the model a strong locality and weight-sharing inductive bias. Stacked convolutional blocks expand the effective receptive field, while strides and stage transitions produce progressively lower-resolution feature maps with increasing channels. The CNN family is broad—including Inception-style multi-path blocks, ResNet, ResNeXt, DenseNet, EfficientNet, and later ConvNeXt-style designs—so comparisons should name the actual backbone rather than treating “CNN” as one fixed model. Their common contribution is a spatially local, hierarchical feature extractor that became the standard computer-vision backbone before transformer alternatives. assertions.source_quote: The CNN mechanism is especially aligned with the structure of many vision tasks. Nearby pixels are usually correlated, and convolution directly encodes that local two-dimensional structure; repeated layers can combine local evidence into larger contexts. Stagewise downsampling also yields a feature pyramid at multiple strides, which detection and segmentation heads can use for small objects, fine boundaries, and semantically coarse regions. assertions.source_quote: DeiT identifies a different route to ViT applicability: data-efficient training and distillation rather than the original very-large-dataset regime. In the taxonomy used by LeViT's discussion, a convolutional teacher helps the transformer student acquire convolutional inductive bias, while stronger augmentation and regularization support training. This demonstrates that plain ViT's data dependence can be mitigated by training design, but it also separates the resulting evidence from the original ViT recipe: a distilled student should not be described as winning solely because of the unchanged architecture. The comparison with CNNs must therefore include the teacher, pretraining corpus, augmentations, and regularization. assertions.source_quote: Battle of the Backbones provides a broader empirical framing of pretraining and architecture. Across its large suite of tasks, datasets, in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, and more than 1,500 training runs, supervised ConvNeXt, supervised SwinV2 trained with ImageNet-21k, and CLIP ViT-Base were highlighted as strong overall choices; the paper also reports that supervised CNNs trained on large sets performed best on most tasks among the models considered. Crucially, the authors attribute part of that supervised advantage to larger training datasets and report that self-supervised models are competitive in apples-to-apples comparisons at similar dataset scale. They also describe ViTs as more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. These are benchmark-specific findings about the included models and protocols, not a timeless ranking of all CNNs against all ViTs. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:ff42df2dd009] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:3a3344a8f9e5]

assertions.source_quote: Dense-prediction boundary of plain ViT. The original ViT was principally a classification architecture over a patch sequence, whereas practical CNN backbones had already been used as multi-scale feature extractors for pixel-level tasks. PVT states this contrast directly: unlike ViT's typically low-resolution outputs and high computational and memory cost, PVT is designed to train on dense image partitions, retain high output resolution, and use progressive shrinking to control the cost of large feature maps. Its transformer feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32 emulate the pyramid interface expected from ResNet-like CNN backbones. PVT is therefore evidence of what plain ViT lacked for dense prediction, not evidence that the original ViT already provided a CNN-style pyramid. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:35a16be2f1a8] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:381624d56a49]

assertions.source_quote: Dense-prediction boundary of plain ViT. The original ViT was principally a classification architecture over a patch sequence, whereas practical CNN backbones had already been used as multi-scale feature extractors for pixel-level tasks. PVT states this contrast directly: unlike ViT's typically low-resolution outputs and high computational and memory cost, PVT is designed to train on dense image partitions, retain high output resolution, and use progressive shrinking to control the cost of large feature maps. Its transformer feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32 emulate the pyramid interface expected from ResNet-like CNN backbones. PVT is therefore evidence of what plain ViT lacked for dense prediction, not evidence that the original ViT already provided a CNN-style pyramid. assertions.source_quote: ViT-CoMer makes the same task-fit distinction from the opposite design direction: it retains a plain pretrained ViT but adds convolutional multi-receptive-field features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion. Its stated motivation is that plain ViT underperforms in dense prediction because it lacks inner-patch information interaction and has limited feature-scale diversity. The method injects a spatial pyramid of convolutional features and fuses hierarchical features across scales so that detection and segmentation can exploit both local and multi-scale information. Its applicability is therefore as an enhanced dense-prediction backbone that depends on added convolutional modules and available ViT pretraining; it should not be conflated with the original ViT baseline. assertions.source_quote: Hierarchical and pooling transformers show how CNN design principles were reintroduced to address plain ViT limitations. HVT progressively pools visual tokens to reduce sequence length, drawing an explicit analogy to CNN feature-map downsampling; this permits scaling depth, width, resolution, or patch size while controlling compute, and its authors report that average-pooled tokens can be more discriminative than a single class token in their experiments. PVT instead builds a transformer pyramid without convolution. These methods preserve transformer-style token processing but modify the original single-sequence design, so their evidence concerns hierarchical transformers rather than plain ViT as originally specified. assertions.source_quote: The unified dynamic-convolution perspective offers an analytical bridge rather than an operational erasure of the architecture distinction. It interprets vision Transformers as ConvNets with input-conditioned dynamic convolutions, allowing attention and dynamic convolution design choices to be compared side by side and enabling designs such as replacing softmax with common ConvNet components or constructing a depth-wise vision Transformer. This helps explain relationships between content-dependent attention and convolution, but the original fixed-kernel CNN backbone still uses locally shared, index-defined kernels, while plain ViT's token mixing is global and content dependent. The appropriate conclusion is conceptual overlap and a shared design space, not identical inductive biases or identical deployment costs. assertions.claim_text: The conceptual overlap does not mean CNNs and plain ViT have identical deployment costs.
assertions.explanation: The paper notes that ViT has quadratic computational complexity and that dynamic convolutions have different efficiency trade-offs, so the conceptual overlap does not mean they have identical deployment costs.

assertions.source_quote: Efficiency mechanisms must be kept distinct from representational mechanisms. Plain global self-attention has cost that grows with the square of token count in the standard formulation, making higher-resolution inputs expensive; the dynamic-convolution survey explicitly identifies this quadratic complexity and slower vanilla-ViT convergence as reasons that CNN modules, pyramids, and local windows were brought back into transformer designs. HVT reduces sequence length through pooling, while LeViT optimizes the speed–accuracy trade-off for fast inference and reports being five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU around 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy. Those efficiency claims belong to modified or hybrid models and specific hardware; they do not imply that the original ViT has the same latency advantage, and FLOPs alone do not determine measured speed. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency mechanisms must be kept distinct from representational mechanisms. Plain global self-attention has cost that grows with the square of token count in the standard formulation, making higher-resolution inputs expensive; the dynamic-convolution survey explicitly identifies this quadratic complexity and slower vanilla-ViT convergence as reasons that CNN modules, pyramids, and local windows were brought back into transformer designs. HVT reduces sequence length through pooling, while LeViT optimizes the speed–accuracy trade-off for fast inference and reports being five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU around 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy. Those efficiency claims belong to modified or hybrid models and specific hardware; they do not imply that the original ViT has the same latency advantage, and FLOPs alone do not determine measured speed. assertions.source_quote: Behavioral applicability also extends beyond aggregate accuracy. A controlled comparative study of ConvNets and ViTs with similar ImageNet accuracy and compute requirements finds differences in error types, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance, including across supervised and CLIP training paradigms. This means that two backbones with the same nominal ImageNet score may not be interchangeable for a specialized application. For the original ViT-versus-CNN question, the practical implication is that mechanism, pretraining, and downstream behavior must all be specified: CNNs provide strong built-in locality and hierarchy, plain ViT provides flexible global token mixing that benefits from scale, and hybrids or adapters are separate attempts to combine those properties. assertions.source_quote: Image classification under different data scales is the pivotal original ViT–CNN comparison. The CvT paper summarizes ViT's empirical regime as follows: a pure Transformer over non-overlapping patch tokens can attain state-of-the-art performance relative to CNNs such as ResNets and EfficientNet when trained on sufficiently large data, including ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, but it remains below similarly sized CNN counterparts when trained on smaller datasets. This is a regime-dependent result rather than a universal winner: a ViT model pretrained on JFT-scale data and a ResNet trained only on ImageNet-1K are not in an apples-to-apples data setting, and neither result should be generalized across both regimes. assertions.source_quote: The LeViT experiments target a different objective: fast inference rather than unconstrained classification accuracy. LeViT is a hybrid that adopts CNN-style decreasing-resolution activation maps and uses attention bias for positional information; near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, the authors report that it is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. Because the metric combines accuracy with measured CPU speed, the result is a speed/accuracy trade-off claim for LeViT and EfficientNet on the stated hardware. It is not a latency comparison between original ViT and generic CNN backbones, and it cannot be inferred from parameter count or FLOPs alone. assertions.source_quote: The LeViT experiments target a different objective: fast inference rather than unconstrained classification accuracy. LeViT is a hybrid that adopts CNN-style decreasing-resolution activation maps and uses attention bias for positional information; near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, the authors report that it is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. Because the metric combines accuracy with measured CPU speed, the result is a speed/accuracy trade-off claim for LeViT and EfficientNet on the stated hardware. It is not a latency comparison between original ViT and generic CNN backbones, and it cannot be inferred from parameter count or FLOPs alone. assertions.source_quote: HVT addresses compute by progressively pooling visual tokens, analogous to CNN downsampling, rather than retaining ViT's full patch sequence throughout inference. On ImageNet and CIFAR-100 image classification, the authors report that HVT outperforms competitive baselines at comparable FLOPs and that average-pooled visual tokens were more discriminative than a single class token in their empirical study. This supports token pooling as a scaling and efficiency mechanism for a hierarchical transformer. It is not a matched result for original ViT versus a CNN, because HVT changes the token sequence and representation hierarchy rather than evaluating the unchanged ViT encoder. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:d55f20aa2f56]

assertions.source_quote: Dense-prediction results expose the clearest task-interface difference. PVT was explicitly built to overcome plain ViT's typically low-resolution output and high computational or memory cost by producing transformer feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32. In its reported COCO object-detection experiment, RetinaNet with PVT achieved 40.4 AP, surpassing RetinaNet with ResNet-50 at 36.3 AP by 4.1 absolute AP at a comparable parameter count. The paper also reports that PVT-Large reached 42.6 AP, 1.6 points above ResNeXt101-64x4d while using 30% fewer parameters. These are matched-task comparisons for PVT versus CNN backbones, but PVT is a pyramid transformer rather than original ViT. assertions.source_quote: Some COCO entries in ViT-CoMer are directly useful as architecture-context comparisons but still depend on pretraining. In the same Mask R-CNN table, InternImage-T reached 49.1% box AP with 49M parameters, ViT-Adapter-T reached 46.0% with 28M, and ViT-CoMer-T reached 47.1% with 29M; at base scale, InternImage-B reached 50.3% with 115M, ViT-Adapter-B reached 49.6% with 120M, and ViT-CoMer-B reached 50.2% with 129M. assertions.source_quote: Representation experiments show that ViTs and ResNets differ even when they solve the same classification task. CKA heatmaps in the controlled analysis found that ViTs had a more uniform internal similarity structure, with greater similarity between lower and higher layers, while ResNet representations were more separated into stages. Cross-model CKA indicated that many lower ResNet layers corresponded to roughly the lowest quarter of ViT layers, and the upper half of ResNet corresponded approximately to the next third of ViT layers; the final third of ViT layers was less similar to ResNet representations. Attention-distance measurements over 5,000 data points further found local and global heads in early ViT layers and global heads at higher layers, unlike early CNN layers with fixed local receptive fields. These are behavioral measurements, not accuracy rankings. assertions.source_quote: Broad backbone benchmarks and behavioral studies argue against selecting a backbone from one ImageNet number. Battle of the Backbones evaluated more than 1,500 runs across classification, detection, out-of-distribution settings and other tasks; within its included model and pretraining suite, supervised ConvNeXt, ImageNet-21k-trained SwinV2, and CLIP ViT-Base were highlighted as strong, while supervised CNNs trained on large datasets performed best on most considered tasks. The authors caution that pretraining-data scale explains part of that outcome and report ViTs to be more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. A separate matched-accuracy, matched-compute comparison finds that ConvNets and ViTs can differ in mistakes, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Thus the experimental conclusion is conditional: CNN backbones show strong built-in locality and dense-prediction compatibility, original ViT is most competitive at adequate scale, and modified transformer results cannot be used as unmatched proof that plain ViT dominates CNNs. assertions.source_quote: Broad backbone benchmarks and behavioral studies argue against selecting a backbone from one ImageNet number. Battle of the Backbones evaluated more than 1,500 runs across classification, detection, out-of-distribution settings and other tasks; within its included model and pretraining suite, supervised ConvNeXt, ImageNet-21k-trained SwinV2, and CLIP ViT-Base were highlighted as strong, while supervised CNNs trained on large datasets performed best on most considered tasks. The authors caution that pretraining-data scale explains part of that outcome and report ViTs to be more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. A separate matched-accuracy, matched-compute comparison finds that ConvNets and ViTs can differ in mistakes, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Thus the experimental conclusion is conditional: CNN backbones show strong built-in locality and dense-prediction compatibility, original ViT is most competitive at adequate scale, and modified transformer results cannot be used as unmatched proof that plain ViT dominates CNNs. assertions.source_quote: Open problems and trade-offs. The first unresolved issue is that architecture, pretraining corpus, and training recipe remain entangled in ViT–CNN comparisons. Plain ViT has fewer vision-specific inductive biases than CNNs, and the cited evidence consistently ties its strongest classification results to sufficiently large data, such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M, or to alternative recipes such as distillation and strong regularization. Battle of the Backbones further reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and model size, while some apparent supervised-model advantages are confounded by larger training sets. The implication is that future comparisons must report data scale, supervision type, distillation teacher, augmentation, regularization, and model capacity together; otherwise a win may describe the training regime rather than the backbone. assertions.source_quote: A second open problem is that ImageNet top-1 accuracy remains an insufficient selection criterion, even after controlling for compute. The Beyond-ImageNet analysis selected ConvNets and ViTs with similar ImageNet accuracy and compute requirements but still found differences in error types, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Battle of the Backbones likewise broadened evaluation to detection, out-of-distribution behavior, and other tasks across more than 1,500 runs. This means that practitioners cannot infer robustness, calibration, or downstream suitability from a single classification score. The open challenge is to establish standardized, task-relevant evaluation suites that distinguish representation quality from nominal accuracy and that avoid overgeneralizing from one benchmark distribution. assertions.source_quote: Plain ViT's dense-prediction interface remains a concrete limitation. The original architecture processes a patch-token sequence for classification and typically lacks the staged, multi-scale feature maps that ResNet-like CNN backbones expose through strides and downsampling. PVT was created because ViT's low-resolution outputs and high computational or memory cost made it difficult to port directly to dense tasks; its pyramid outputs at strides 4, 8, 16, and 32 were needed to emulate a CNN backbone interface. ViT-CoMer similarly identifies limited inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity as reasons plain ViT underperforms in detection and segmentation. The trade-off is therefore not merely accuracy: using plain ViT for pixel-level tasks may require adapters, pyramids, convolutional features, or a redesigned detection head.
